title: Potato vs Sweet Potato: Nutrition Differences

seo.title: Potato vs Sweet Potato: Calories, Fiber and Nutrients
seo.meta_description: Potatoes and sweet potatoes have very similar calories and carbs. Orange sweet potato stands out for beta-carotene; potato often provides more potassium.
seo.search_intent: Compare cooked potato and sweet potato without exaggerating small calorie and carbohydrate differences.

excerpt: Potatoes and sweet potatoes are much closer in calories and carbohydrate than their reputations suggest: both are around 90 calories and 20–21 grams of carbohydrate per 100 grams cooked. Orange sweet potatoes stand out for beta-carotene; potatoes often provide more potassium and slightly more protein.
content_html:
Sweet potatoes are often presented as a healthier replacement for white potatoes, but calories and carbohydrate barely separate the two. The more interesting differences are micronutrients.

At the same cooked weight, both are around 90 calories per 100 grams. Orange sweet potato stands out for provitamin-A carotenoids, while potato often provides more potassium and vitamin C depending on preparation.

A cooked comparison per 100 grams

PotatoOrange sweet potato
Calories~90–95~90
Carbohydrate~21 g~21 g
Protein~2–2.5 g~2 g
Fiber~2 g~3 g

Energy and carbohydrate are essentially tied. Sweet potato may provide about 1 extra gram of fiber per 100 grams, while potato has a small protein edge that is unlikely to change a meal.

The orange color marks a real nutritional difference

Orange-fleshed sweet potatoes are concentrated in beta-carotene, which the body can convert to vitamin A. A normal serving can provide several times the daily reference amount of provitamin A.

White and purple sweet potatoes do not have the same carotenoid profile, so ‘sweet potato’ does not describe one identical nutrient composition either.

Potato often provides more potassium

A cooked potato with skin can exceed 500 mg of potassium per 100 grams, while sweet potato is often closer to 300–400 mg. Across a 7-ounce serving, the difference can exceed 200 mg.

Cooking method matters: boiling and discarding the water can reduce potassium in either tuber.

Vitamin C often favors potato

Potatoes contribute vitamin C, although storage and long cooking can reduce it. Sweet potatoes provide some too, but often less in comparable varieties and preparations.

Sweet taste does not mean dramatically more carbohydrate

During cooking, enzymes and heat can turn some sweet-potato starch into sugars, making it taste sweeter. The total carbohydrate per 100 grams still remains very close to potato.

Taste alone does not reveal how many calories a food contains.

Frying changes more than choosing one tuber over the other

Both absorb oil and lose water when fried. French fries or sweet-potato chips can easily exceed 300 calories per 100 grams compared with roughly 90 when baked or boiled with little added fat.

The cooking method can create a far larger energy difference than the choice of tuber.

The useful rule

Potatoes and sweet potatoes are practically tied in calories and carbs. Orange sweet potato stands out for beta-carotene and somewhat more fiber; potato often provides more potassium and vitamin C. Alternating them brings more variety than trying to crown one universally healthier.

faq.question: Which has more calories, potato or sweet potato?
faq.answer: Cooked with little added fat, they are essentially tied at around 90 calories per 100 grams.

faq.question: Does sweet potato have more sugar?
faq.answer: It tastes sweeter because some starch is converted to sugars during cooking, but total carbohydrate is very similar to potato.

faq.question: Which has more vitamin A?
faq.answer: Orange-fleshed sweet potato by a very large margin because it is rich in beta-carotene.
